value: Writing things down clears your mind. Use the Notes section to 'brain dump' everything that's worrying you.
Journaling is a great way to clear your head. Just tell me 'Add note: My day was...' and I'll save it for you securely.

Checking the note content...

Zettelkasten is a method where you write one idea per note and link them together. It turns your notes into a 'Second Brain' that grows with you.
The Cornell Method uses three sections: Cues, Notes, and Summary. It's excellent for active recall and studying complex topics.
Mind Mapping is a visual way to organize information. Start with a central concept and branch out to related ideas to see the big picture.
Progressive Summarization involves reviewing notes in layers: bolding the best parts, then highlighting the 'best of the best'. It makes info easy to find later.
During brainstorming, focus on quantity over quality. Write every single idea down in a quick note without judging it—you can prune them later.
First Principles thinking means breaking a problem down to its most basic truths and building up from there. Use a note to map out these foundational elements.
Inversion is the art of thinking backwards. Instead of 'How can I succeed?', ask 'How could I fail?' and write down how to avoid those pitfalls.
To beat writer's block, try 'Free Writing': set a timer for 5 minutes and write whatever comes to mind in a note without stopping. Don't worry about grammar!
Use tags or categories to group related notes. A good system is PARA: Projects, Areas, Resources, and Archives.
Linking notes allows you to navigate between related concepts. It helps you find 'hidden' connections between different projects or ideas.
Pin your most important notes (like your current goals or a daily checklist) to the top of the list so they're always visible.
Schedule a weekly review to go through your 'Inbox' of quick notes. File them into categories, add detail, or delete what you no longer need.
You can capture ideas hands-free! Just tap the mic icon and say 'Take a note: [Your Idea]' and I'll transcribe and save it for you.
Speed is key for ideation. Use the Home screen search bar or the '+' button to capture thoughts before they disappear.
Try these prompts: 'What am I grateful for today?', 'What is my #1 priority?', or 'What did I learn today?'
A 'Brain Dump' is when you write every single task, worry, and idea in your head into one long note. It's the fastest way to reduce mental stress.
For effective meeting minutes, focus on: Participants, Decisions Made, and Action Items. Assign owners and deadlines to those actions immediately.
A project roadmap note should outline your Vision, Milestones, and potential Blockers. Use sub-features to track progress through each stage.
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) are step-by-step guides for recurring tasks. Documenting them saves you mental energy every time you repeat the process.
Brevity is power. Try to summarize your ideas in 3 bullet points. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough yet.
Use notes for active recall: write down questions about a topic, then try to answer them from memory before checking your study materials.
Summarizing a long note helps solidify your understanding. Try the 'One Sentence Summary' challenge for every article you read.
An outline is the skeleton of your thoughts. Start with your main points as headers, then fill in the details under each one.
The app can automatically archive or delete unpinned notes after a certain time. Check your Note Settings to keep your workspace clean.
Your notes are stored in an encrypted local database. Your private journals and business ideas are protected by your device's security.
You can export your notes as JSON in Data Management. It's a good practice to keep a backup of your 'Second Brain' occasionally.
I can search through your note titles and content instantly. Just use the search bar or ask me 'Find the note about...'
Gratitude journaling retrains your brain to see the positive. Write down 3 small things that went well today—it takes less than a minute!
A learning log is a place to document what you've learned each day. It turns passive information into active, usable knowledge.
To start a dream journal, keep your phone by your bed. As soon as you wake up, use a quick note to capture every detail you remember.
End your month with a reflection note: What were my wins? What were my losses? What will I change next month?
When reading, don't just highlight. Write a note in your own words explaining the 'Why' behind the author's point. That's where true learning happens.
Try a '100-word limit' for your ideas. Constraints force you to be more creative and focus only on the most essential information.
Keep a note of your favorite Mental Models (like Occam's Razor or Compounding). Review them before making any major life decisions.
Digital minimalism in notes means keeping only what is actionable or truly inspirational. If a note doesn't serve a purpose, delete it.
Use templates for recurring notes like Daily Standups or Gym Logs. It ensures you capture all the right data every single time.
Archive notes you might need in the future; delete notes that were just temporary 'scratches'. Archives keep your history without the clutter.
Before a deep work session, write down exactly what you intend to accomplish. Having a physical note of your goal prevents 'goal drift'.
When brainstorming solo, try the 'Six Thinking Hats' method. Switch between different perspectives (logical, emotional, creative) in separate notes.
Your external brain (this app) is more reliable than your biological one for storage. Trust the system to hold the info so your mind can do the thinking.
A Commonplace Book is a central note where you collect quotes, snippets, and ideas from other people that resonate with you.
Interstitial journaling means writing a few sentences every time you switch tasks. It tracks your time and helps you refocus faster.
Don't over-complicate your folders. Use broad categories and rely on our powerful search feature to find specific details instantly.
Writing is thinking on paper. If you're confused about a problem, start writing about it. The act of forming sentences often reveals the solution.
Morning Pages are three pages of long-form, stream-of-consciousness writing done first thing in the morning. Use a note to clear your 'mental fog'.
Use bullet points for lists and actions; use paragraphs for deep reflections. Mixing styles helps you scan notes quickly while keeping depth where needed.
Every morning, create a 'Daily Mission' note with just one objective. If you do nothing else today, making progress on that one thing is a win.
